cards.explanation: The answer is Saul. Verse 1 says the LORD delivered David “…from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.” The song names Saul right alongside all the rest. Saul was Israel's king, the one Samuel was sent to anoint (1 Samuel 15:1).

The answer is places to stay safe. David even says “…in whom I take refuge…” in verse 3. Rock, fortress, stronghold and refuge are all spots you run to when trouble's chasing you, friends. Picture a hole in a cliff, and you've got the idea.

The answer is saved. David says, “I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies.” That's David speaking about himself. He says he will call, and he says he will be saved.

The answer is that he cries out to the LORD. Verse 7 says, “In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God.” David is entangled in the cords of Sheol, and the song says he cries out to God. That's a good thing for all of us to remember on a tangled-up day.
The answer is False. David says, “And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears.” The cry reached God. Nothing got lost in the mail, friends.

The answer is that the LORD burned with anger. Verse 8 says the earth shook and quaked, “they were shaken because He burned with anger.” David gives the reason in the same verse. The shaking comes from the LORD Himself.
The answer is True. Verse 11 says, “He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind.” That's David's picture of the LORD coming to rescue him.
The answer is False. The foes don't hold their ground. Verse 15 says, “He shot His arrows and scattered the foes…” They're scattered and routed.

The answer is that He reaches down and draws him out. Verse 17 says, “He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters.” David was in the waves of death, and the LORD took hold of him personally. That's a mighty close rescue, friends.
The answer is because He delighted in him. David says, “He rescued me because He delighted in me.” That's the reason, right there in verse 20. Being delighted in is a sweet thing to hear.

The answer is that he kept the ways of the LORD. David says in verse 22, “For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God.” That's what he points to. It's about staying on the LORD's path.

The answer is False. In verse 23, David says, “For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes.” He's keeping them in front of him. Setting them aside is the opposite of what he sings.
The answer is True. Verse 26 says, “To the faithful You show Yourself faithful…” David sings it to God, and the verse says “You.” So the statement is true just as written.

The answer is False. Verse 27 says, “…but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd.” The word at the end is shrewd, not crooked. The lines before it follow a pattern, friends, but this one changes at that spot.

The answer is to bring them down. Verse 28 says, “You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.” The afflicted get saved, and the haughty get brought down. David puts both in one breath.

The answer is charge an army and scale a wall. David sings, “For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall.” Charging an army and climbing a wall both look like jobs for a crowd, and he says he can do them in God. Me, I'd need a ladder, a pep talk and a nap.

The answer is that there is no one else. Verse 32 asks, “For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?” Those are questions with an obvious answer, and David's answer is nobody. The LORD stands alone in the song.
The answer is battle. David says, “He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze.” It's the LORD who does the training, friends.
The answer is True. Verse 35 says, “my arms can bend a bow of bronze.” David sings it right after saying the LORD trains his hands for battle.

The answer is God's gentleness. David says to the LORD, “…Your gentleness exalts me.” Right in the middle of all that battle talk, a soft word like gentleness shows up. It's the kind of detail you'd miss if you were rushing, bakers.

The answer is False. Verse 37 says, “You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way.” The path gets wider, and his ankles do not give way. So the second half of that statement is the part that's off.
The answer is strength. David says to the LORD, “You have armed me with strength for battle…” The strength comes from God. David sings it as a gift.
The answer is False. Verse 42 says of the enemies, “They looked, but there was no one to save them…” and then says they looked to the LORD, but He did not answer. So no answer comes to them.
The answer is strife. David says to the LORD, “You have delivered me from the strife of my people…” This verse names his own people. Strife is the word that fills the blank.

The answer is that they cower and obey him. Verse 45 says, “Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me.” Cowering and obeying, both in one verse. David sings it as part of what the LORD has done for him.
The answer is False. Verse 48 praises “…the God who avenges me and brings down nations beneath me…” The nations go beneath David, not above him. So the statement has it backward, friends.

The answer is praise the LORD and sing to His name. David says, “Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name.” After the rescue comes the praise. This song is part of it.

The answer is David and his descendants forever. David closes with, “He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.” It's not only David, and it's not only his lifetime. The song ends on forever.

The answer is True. Verse 51 says, “He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.” David is the anointed one the song names. That's right there in the song's closing words.
